hero.title: Dementia Risk Assessment
hero.desc: Integrating veteran commentator Ma Hsi-ping's 10-year personal battle against dementia, along with international research from The Lancet, Harvard, and Finland. A 3-minute self-assessment with 10 lifestyle prescriptions.
hero.src: Source: "Pao-chieh Health Talk" 2026.05.23 · Compiled by NotebookLM
hero.disclaimer: ⚠️ This assessment is a health education self-screening tool and cannot replace medical diagnosis. If you have concerns, please visit a neurologist or memory clinic. AD8 scale results are for reference only.

tabs.edu: ⑤ Health Education · Dementia Facts You Didn't Know

ad8.title: AD8 Very Early Dementia Screening
ad8.sub: Think about changes compared to the past (over the past few years). Have the following situations "changed"? Can be answered by yourself or a family member who knows you well.
questions: Problems with judgment (falling for scams, poor financial decisions, buying inappropriate gifts)
Reduced interest in activities and hobbies
Repeating the same questions, stories, or statements
Difficulty learning to use tools / appliances / electronics (TV, washing machine, microwave, remote control, etc.)
Forgetting the correct month or year
Difficulty handling complex finances (forgetting to pay bills, file taxes, manage accounts)
Persistent problems with thinking or memory
ad8.ok: No significant concerns at this time
ad8.advice: AD8 is an internationally used very early screening tool. 2 or more items changed indicates that cognitive function may already be affected. Prompt medical evaluation is recommended.

risk.title: The Lancet 14 Modifiable Risk Factors
risk.sub: The 2024 Lancet Commission on Dementia Prevention identified: eliminating these 14 risk factors could prevent or delay approximately 45% of dementia cases. Check the items that currently apply to you.
factors: The #1 risk factor; prolonged headphone use, untreated hearing impairment without hearing aids
Newly added in 2024; tied for #1 this year
Lack of learning and mental engagement after middle age
Newly added in 2024; untreated cataracts, etc.
History of head impact or concussion
Poor blood sugar and blood pressure control
Active smoking or long-term secondhand smoke exposure
Uncontrolled high blood pressure in midlife
Depression, panic disorder, chronic high stress
Living alone, rarely interacting with others
risk.advice: Every single factor is modifiable. The more that apply, the more worthwhile it is to start adjusting with the "③ Lifestyle Prescriptions."

rx.title: Ma Hsi-ping's 10 Lifestyle Prescriptions
rx.sub: Based on The Lancet's 14 factors, Harvard's 43-year follow-up, and Finland's multi-domain lifestyle intervention studies. Doing all of them can delay/prevent dementia by over 45%. Check the items you are "already doing."
items: 🧩 Mental stimulation
Chess, bridge, learning new things — activating brain cells and the hippocampus
🚶 Regular exercise
Continuous walking ≥15 minutes per day, accumulating 3,000–7,500 steps (3,000 steps delays by 3 years, 7,500 steps caps at 7 years)
🥗 Healthy diet
Mediterranean diet: more fish, more vegetables, use good oils (olive oil)
🗣️ Social interaction
Regularly chatting and socializing with others, avoiding social isolation
📖 Continuous learning
Never stop learning; attend senior universities, join clubs (especially important for women)
🚭 Quit smoking, reduce alcohol
Quit smoking and reduce alcohol consumption
☕ Moderate tea and coffee
Coffee delays by 18%, tea by 14%, both together by 34%; coffee ≤3 cups per day, avoid hot drinks in plastic cups
💼 Delay retirement
Each year of delayed retirement reduces dementia risk by 3.2%; retiring at 60 vs. 65 differs by about 43%
😴 Good sleep + weight control
Deep sleep "brain wash" clears waste; use sleep aids cautiously, control obesity
💕 Happy dopamine

Do things that make you happy (exercise, running, falling in love, emotional connections) — a dopamine surge can prevent Parkinson's disease. Ma Hsi-ping's father dated from age 90 to 100, keeping his mind sharp and dementia-free
rx.advice: The more you do, the stronger your brain protection. Items you haven't started are your next step.

edu.title: Health Education · Dementia Facts You Didn't Know
edu.sub: Excerpted from Ma Hsi-ping's interview on "Pao-chieh Health Talk" and international research.

cards.title: ⏳ Dementia Timeline
cards.body: From the initial accumulation of "bad proteins" (β-amyloid deposits) in the brain to the onset of mild dementia, there is an approximately 20-year latency period. This 20-year window is the golden period for prevention.
cards.note: Aging → (memory loss / Mild Cognitive Impairment MCI, an intermediate stage between aging and dementia) → dementia. Ma Hsi-ping describes himself as having "moderate memory loss, severe but not yet dementia."

cards.title: 🚨 Early Warning Signs (Ma Hsi-ping's Personal Experience)
list: Watched a movie in the theater, but had absolutely no memory of it when re-watching at home on TV
Unable to name objects, can only say "that thing, that thing" (couldn't say "egg tart")
Read a book before bed, but the next day couldn't recall where they left off
Couldn't recite Tang dynasty poems that were memorized since childhood
Could only remember "Makro" (a store that no longer exists) when thinking of hypermarkets
Couldn't remember friends' or students' names
180-degree personality reversal (gentle becoming violent) — a frightening sign of frontotemporal dementia

cards.title: 👂 Three Major "Sensory" Warning Signs (Most Easily Overlooked)
cards.note: Because the eyes, ears, and teeth are closest to the brain, their deterioration directly impacts cognition.
ranks: Young people who listen to loud music with headphones for extended periods are a high-risk group.
The optic nerve is closest to the brain's neural pathways.
Japanese research: having fewer than 20 teeth increases dementia risk 5-fold. Japan promotes the "8020 Plan" (keeping 20 teeth at age 80, including dentures).

cards.title: 🩺 Detection Methods
list: MRI / CT scan: Can only detect moderate to severe stages (often too late to reverse)
PET scan: Can detect mild stages, costs approximately NT$60,000
Blood test: Approved by the U.S. FDA this year, costs approximately NT$20,000 (latest development)

cards.title: 💊 New Treatment Developments
list: Monoclonal antibodies (lecanemab / donanemab): Clear amyloid proteins; one course costs approximately NT$1.5 million, requires 12–18 months of treatment, and only about 14% of patients are eligible (to avoid cerebral hemorrhage / cerebral edema).

National Brain Cleanse No. 1: Developed by Taiwan's Ministry of Health and Welfare, National Research Institute of Chinese Medicine. Has successfully cleared amyloid proteins in mice and monkeys; human trials are underway.
"Brain wash" mechanism: During deep sleep, brain cells shrink to create gaps, allowing cerebrospinal fluid to flush out amyloid and other waste. Sleep is nature's free cleaner.

cards.title: 📊 Taiwan's Dementia Tsunami
stats: Enters super-aged society in December (fastest in the world, only 7 years)
Dementia rate among those 65+, doubling within 10 years
cards.note: Women face higher risk, partly due to less social engagement and fewer learning opportunities — making "continuous learning and social interaction" especially important for women.

cards.title: 💕 Dopamine and Parkinson's Disease
cards.body: Parkinson's disease is caused by insufficient dopamine in the brain, which can further lead to dementia symptoms. Ma Hsi-ping points out that the best "daily prescription" is to actively engage in activities that bring happiness and trigger massive dopamine release (a dopamine surge).
cards.subTitle: Specific Lifestyle Prescriptions
subList: Exercise and running: Naturally stimulate dopamine production in the brain through physical activity.
Falling in love and emotional connections: Keeping emotions active effectively stimulates the brain. Any activity that brings joy and pleasure is helpful.
cards.caseBody: Ma Hsi-ping's father started dating at age 90 and continued until age 100. Dating triggered a massive dopamine surge in his brain, keeping his mind sharp and effectively preventing dementia.
cards.note: 💡 For Parkinson's disease patients, the most important concept is to encourage them to find and participate in activities that make them happy, naturally replenishing the dopamine their brain lacks through joyful emotions.

media.transcriptSub: Compiled by NotebookLM from the interview into structured key points (medical data preserved)

transcriptSections.title: 1. Taiwan's Aging Crisis and Dementia Tsunami
transcriptSections.body: Taiwan has the world's fastest aging population: it entered an aging society in 1993, became an aged society in 2018, and by the end of 2025 will enter a "super-aged society" with over 20% of the population aged 65+, taking only 7 years from aged to super-aged. Government projections suggest the total population may halve to 12 million by 2065. Currently about 8% of those over 60 have dementia, expected to double within 10 years; women (9.35%) have a higher rate than men (6.36%).

transcriptSections.title: 2. Dementia Timeline and the Golden 20-Year Latency Period
transcriptSections.body: From mild dementia to death takes approximately 3–10 years. But from the brain's initial accumulation of "β-amyloid protein" to the onset of mild dementia, there is a 20-year latency period — this is the golden window for prevention, delay, and even stopping the disease. Memory loss (MCI, Mild Cognitive Impairment) is the intermediate stage between aging and dementia.

transcriptSections.title: 3. Early Warning Signs: "Brain Blackout" Phenomena
list: Short-term memory cannot be retained: No memory of a movie just watched in the theater; can't recall what was read before bed the next day.

Forgetting familiar words: Knowing what an object looks like but unable to name it (can only say "that thing" instead of "egg tart"); only remembering "Makro" (a defunct store) when thinking of hypermarkets.

Long-term memory and face recognition difficulties: Suddenly unable to recite well-memorized Tang dynasty poems; cannot recall familiar people's names, resorting to indirect conversation to confirm identity.

transcriptSections.title: 4. Sensory Warning Signs: Hearing, Vision, and Teeth
list: Hearing loss: Listed by The Lancet as the #1 dementia risk factor. Prolonged loud headphone use is high risk.
Fewer than 20 teeth: Japanese Ministry of Health research shows dementia risk increases over 5-fold, hence the "8020 Plan" (including dentures).
Vision decline: The optic nerve is close to brain neural pathways; vision impairment is also a significant risk factor.

transcriptSections.title: 5. Hidden Killers in Daily Life
list: Environmental toxins: Heavy metals and PM2.5 can enter the brain; microplastics are called a "super killer" (hot coffee in paper cups, hot food in plastic bags, bottled water).
High LDL cholesterol: Latest research ranks it tied for #1 with hearing loss.
Mood and medication: Chronic stress, panic, depression, excessive sleep medication, and general anesthesia all damage brain cells.
Micronutrient deficiency: Both B12 and lithium deficiency can trigger dementia.
Head injury: Head impacts have documented cases of causing cognitive impairment.

transcriptSections.title: 6. The "10 Lifestyle Interventions" That Can Change Your Fate (Can Delay/Prevent >45%)
list: Continuous learning: Not learning has been repeatedly listed as the #1 or #2 risk factor.
Delayed retirement: Brain cells begin shrinking around age 60; retiring at 60 carries 43% higher risk than retiring at 65; each year of delayed retirement reduces dementia risk by 3.2%.
Continuous walking: Accumulating 3,000 steps daily delays by 3 years, 7,500 steps delays by 7 years (maximum), but each session must be at least 15 continuous minutes.
Social interaction: The brains of socially isolated elderly remain chronically inactive, with extremely high dementia risk.
Tea and coffee: Coffee delays by 18%, tea by 14%, both together by 34%; coffee ≤3 cups per day.
Continuous mental engagement: Chess, bridge, and mahjong maintain neuronal activity.
Healthy diet + weight control: Mediterranean diet, good oils (olive oil), avoid obesity.
Address sleep disorders: Deep sleep activates the brain's self-cleaning mechanism.
Quit smoking, reduce alcohol: Reduces neuroinflammation.

transcriptSections.title: 7. Detection Methods and New Treatment Developments
list: Detection: MRI / PET scan (approx. NT$60,000) → latest blood test (approx. NT$20,000, FDA-approved) enables early detection.
"Brain wash" mechanism: During deep sleep, brain cells shrink to create gaps, allowing cerebrospinal fluid to flush out amyloid protein; insomnia disrupts this detox process.

Monoclonal antibody drugs: Can clear amyloid proteins; one course takes 12–18 months, costs approximately NT$1.5 million, and only about 14% are eligible (to prevent cerebral hemorrhage / cerebral edema).

National Brain Cleanse No. 1: Developed by Taiwan's Ministry of Health and Welfare, National Research Institute of Chinese Medicine; animal studies have confirmed amyloid protein clearance; preparing for technology transfer and drug approval application.

transcriptSections.title: 8. The Link Between Dopamine and Parkinson's Disease
transcriptSections.body: Parkinson's disease is caused by insufficient dopamine in the brain, which can further lead to dementia symptoms. Ma Hsi-ping points out that the best "daily prescription" is to actively engage in activities that bring happiness and trigger a dopamine "surge."
list: Exercise and running: Naturally stimulate dopamine production in the brain through physical activity.

Falling in love and emotional connections: Keeping emotions active effectively stimulates the brain. Ma Hsi-ping's father started dating at age 90 and continued until age 100, experiencing a massive dopamine surge that kept his mind sharp and successfully prevented dementia.
transcriptSections.conclusion: Conclusion: Encourage Parkinson's disease patients to find and participate in activities that make them happy, naturally replenishing the dopamine their brain lacks through joyful emotions.

selfcheck.title: AD8 Screening Advanced
selfcheck.sub: Separates "symptom warnings" from "risk factors" for more precise interpretation than a single total score. Select "Yes" if applicable, "No" if not.
selfcheck.warnSub: Have you experienced cognitive changes recently? If multiple answers are "Yes," the clinical significance is usually greater than the total score alone.
selfcheck.riskSub: Currently known important risk factors and modifiable elements.
selfcheck.adviceLow: Overall risk is currently low. Continue maintaining brain health. Keep up exercise, social interaction, and good sleep habits.
selfcheck.adviceMid: Several modifiable factors have been identified. Prioritize addressing sleep, exercise, metabolic health, and sensory issues. Monitor for symptom changes.
selfcheck.adviceHigh: Both symptom warnings and risk factors are elevated. Scheduling a neurology or memory clinic evaluation is recommended.
selfcheck.warnNote: ⚠️ If 2 or more symptom warning questions are "Yes," or if they are already affecting work, finances, medication management, navigation, or conversation, a neurology / memory clinic evaluation is recommended.
selfcheck.bandLowDesc: Overall risk is currently low. Continue maintaining brain health.
selfcheck.bandMidDesc: Several modifiable factors identified. Prioritize addressing sleep, exercise, metabolic health, and sensory issues.
selfcheck.bandHighDesc: Early formal evaluation is recommended, especially if symptom warning scores are high.

questions.text: You have been frequently forgetting things that just happened recently, such as content you just read or things you just said, and it is noticeably worse than before.
questions.help: The key is whether it has "recently become noticeable" and occurs repeatedly.

questions.text: Difficulty finding words or naming common objects has been happening more frequently than before.
questions.help: Occasionally forgetting a word is common; it becomes notable when it's increasingly frequent and affects conversation.

questions.text: When seeing familiar people, you often can't recall their names, or you become confused about familiar faces and relationships.
questions.help: A momentary lapse isn't necessarily abnormal; the key is whether it's increasing and affecting interactions.

questions.text: You get more easily confused doing familiar tasks, such as making payments, organizing documents, or performing familiar procedures.
questions.help: Changes in these functional abilities are clinically more significant than inability to recall old information.

questions.text: Others have noticed that your memory, judgment, conversation, or work efficiency has recently declined.
questions.help: Observations from others are often an important clue.

questions.text: The above situations have begun affecting your work, finances, medication management, navigation, or daily planning.
questions.help: If so, seeking medical evaluation is recommended.

questions.text: You have hearing loss, severe tinnitus, or frequently can't hear clearly but haven't addressed it.
questions.help: Hearing problems are one of the most important modifiable risk factors.

questions.text: You have vision deterioration or eye disease, and your current correction or treatment is insufficient.
questions.help: Untreated vision problems are also associated with increased dementia risk.

questions.text: You have high LDL, high triglycerides, diabetes, hypertension, or cardiovascular disease.
questions.help: Cardiometabolic control is highly related to brain health.

questions.text: You usually don't get enough exercise — for example, most days you don't walk briskly for at least 15 continuous minutes.
questions.help: Regular physical activity is associated with cognitive protection.

questions.text: You have chronic poor sleep, or possibly have sleep apnea or severe daytime sleepiness.
questions.help: Sleep problems can be both a risk factor and affect current cognitive performance.

questions.text: You have been under chronic stress, depression, anxiety, or significant emotional distress.
questions.help: Emotional state and cognitive performance often affect each other.

questions.text: You smoke, are obese, or have a diet chronically high in saturated fat and low in fruits and vegetables.
questions.help: Start by adjusting one or two actionable habits.

questions.text: You interact with others infrequently, and your social activities in the past year have been significantly insufficient.
questions.help: Insufficient social stimulation is associated with cognitive decline risk.

questions.text: You have had a head injury, especially a concussion or impact that caused symptoms.
questions.help: Head injury is a known risk factor.

questions.text: Your current medications, B12 deficiency, thyroid issues, or other physical conditions may be causing memory or attention decline.
questions.help: These conditions are often reversible causes and worth mentioning proactively during medical visits.

selfcheck.disclaimer: ⚠️ Based on publicly available medical data: early warning signs reference the Alzheimer's Association and CDC; risk factors reference Lancet 2024; clinical evaluation references the Mayo Clinic MCI guidelines. This tool is for self-assessment only and does not replace diagnosis.
